heroSub: People ever born on Earth. PRB estimate, carried forward at today’s birth rate. It grows every second.
bornSince: Born since you opened this page
diedSince: Died since you opened this page
calTitle: The last hour of Earth’s year
calNote: If Earth’s 4.54 billion years were one calendar year, the whole human story happens on the night of December 31.
calPre: The genus Homo begins at 18:36 the same day
calCh1: Chapter 1 of this game (120,000–50,000 years ago)
sibBtn: Be born as a younger sibling
autoHint: Auto will choose in a moment · tap to choose yourself
ch1t: Many kinds of human: when we were not alone
ch1d: Several human species share the world. An ice age is coming and Toba is about to erupt. Who will you be born as?
ch2t: The farming revolution: from foraging to the first fields
ch2d: Try taming wild animals, sow the first fields and settle villages. A herd is food, labour, wealth and standing, across eight lands from the Levant to Spirit Cave.
chNwT: The New World: from Columbus to the Civil War (Thai only)
chNwD: This chapter is in Thai only for now. Three hundred and seventy years in which people from three continents met on one land, from Columbus, Tenochtitlan, the Inca and Potosí to Plymouth, the first Thanksgiving, the American and Haitian revolutions and the end of slavery.
chMoT: The Mongol Empire: from the steppe to the Black Death (Thai only)
chMoD: This chapter is in Thai only for now. Two hundred years in which fewer than a million people from the steppe changed the world, from Temüjin to Karakorum, Dadu, Hangzhou, Kyiv, Tabriz, Caffa and the plague.
chIsT: The Islamic golden age: Baghdad, the House of Wisdom and the Mongols (Thai only)
chIsD: This chapter is in Thai only for now. Five hundred years of the Arabic-speaking world, from round Baghdad, paper and the House of Wisdom to Córdoba, Cairo, Bukhara, the Crusades and the Mongols.
chSuT: Suvarnabhumi: Funan, Dvaravati and Si Thep to Sukhothai
chSuD: Be born in twelve hundred years of the land that became Thailand and its neighbours, from the ports of Funan, Dvaravati and Si Thep to the stone sanctuaries of Angkor and the founding of Sukhothai. Watch the Golden Boy being cast, help raise the Phanom Rung lintel, feed the house spirits, and see how Mon, Khmer, Malay and Tai people mixed into the people of this region.
chGaT: The Ganges: the age of the Buddha and Ashoka
chGaD: Be born in six hundred years of the Ganges valley, from the sixteen realms to the writing down of the scriptures. Feed teachers of many schools, Buddhist, Jain, Ajivika and Brahmin, leave milk for the nagas, watch Ashoka carve his edicts, and see how a story grows as it is retold.
chRoT: Rome: from Hannibal’s elephants to the last emperor
chRoD: Be born somewhere in seven hundred years of the Roman world, from the wars with Carthage to an empire split in two. Watch Caesar cross the Rubicon, hear the teacher from Nazareth, sweat it out under Vesuvius, train for Olympia, and choose between beer and wine.
chGrT: The Greeks: from Homer and democracy to the coming of Rome
chGrD: Be born in one of a thousand city-states round a sea that burst in five million years ago. Get cornered by Socrates in the market, row at Salamis, choose a saying to live by, and see who really got a vote in the first democracy.
chOlT: The Olmec: colossal stone heads and rubber balls
chOlD: Drag basalt boulders of tens of tons with no wheels and no draft animals, carve a ruler’s face, meet tapirs, jaguars and howler monkeys, and find out why this continent had no horses or oxen.
chShT: Shang China: turtle shells that question the ancestors
chShD: Crack turtle shells with fire to question the ancestors, cast the greatest bronzes in the world, march with Fu Hao, and see the dynasty fall at Muye. The signs you carve still live on in Chinese writing today.
chAeT: The Aegean: Minoan palaces, the Thera eruption and the Bronze Age collapse
chAeD: Palaces without walls on Crete, the eruption of Thera, Mycenaean palace accounts, ships laden with copper, and then a whole connected world around the sea falling apart within a few decades.
chInT: The Indus: great cities whose script no one can read
chInD: Grid-planned brick cities, covered drains, seals, and a script no one can read. Look for traces of an ancient faith that scholars still argue about today.
chEgT: Egypt: life by the Nile in the shadow of the pyramids
chEgD: The yearly flood rules your life. Pyramids, hieroglyphs, papyrus, hippos, crocodiles and the weighing of the heart. You live as long as your name is spoken.
ch3t: Mesopotamia: cuneiform, beer and the laws of Hammurabi
ch3d: The first cities, the first writing, bronze, beer, Hammurabi’s laws, the Epic of Gilgamesh and the Hanging Gardens. Your name is written in clay.
chMamT: The Ice Age: mammoth hunters and painted caves
chMamD: The height of the Ice Age. The mammoth steppe spans continents; people invent needles, bows and spear-throwers, then walk a land bridge to America.
noTools: No new tools yet. Choose “Practice skills” to learn.
learned: You learn to make {t} from others in the band
firstInvent: You are the first in your band to make {t}
src9: Chapter 3: dates for the first herding and farming in each region are estimates from archaeology and DNA and still debated. Animal loans, marriage gifts and rumours are simulated from later societies, and the game squeezes many generations of domestication into one life.
src6: Chapter 2: when people reached the Americas, and the age of several tools, are still debated. The game uses the ranges most evidence supports.
chPacT: Pacific voyagers: reading the stars across the ocean
chPacD: Sail double-hulled canoes from island to island, steering by stars, swells and birds, all the way to Hawaiʻi, Rapa Nui and Aotearoa.
chJT: Out of Africa: a 60,000-year line of travellers
chJD: Begin in East Africa about 70,000 years ago. Each time you die, continue as a descendant generations later and choose where the line goes: Europe, Asia, Sahul, or across Beringia to America.

src7: Pacific chapter: arrival dates follow the ranges most radiocarbon studies accept. The islanders’ “1 in X” against world population is a rough estimate.
src10: Chapter 04, Mesopotamia: the law codes of Ur-Nammu and Hammurabi, Nanni’s letter to the merchant Ea-nasir (British Museum), and Sumerian literature from the ETCSL database (University of Oxford). Names follow real name patterns; cuneiform spellings are approximate.
src11: Chapter 05, Egypt: the Westcar Papyrus (Egyptian Museum, Berlin), the diary of Merer from Wadi al-Jarf, excavations of the Giza workers’ town (Mark Lehner, AERA), and records of the Deir el-Medina workmen’s village. Names and hieroglyphs follow real name patterns.
src12: Chapter 06, Indus: harappa.com (J. M. Kenoyer), the Penn Museum, Robbins Schug et al. (2013, PLOS ONE) on disease and violence at Harappa, Shinde et al. (2019, Cell) on Rakhigarhi DNA, and Petrie et al. (2017, Current Anthropology) on crops and the monsoon. The game’s signs only imitate shapes.
src13: Chapter 07, Aegean: Linear B tablets (Ventris and Chadwick, Documents in Mycenaean Greek), letters from Ugarit, the Uluburun wreck (Cemal Pulak, INA), Eric H. Cline (1177 B.C.), and Knapp and Manning (2016) on climate and the collapse. The date of the Thera eruption is still debated.
src23: Chapter 16, the New World (Thai only): Sahagún’s Florentine Codex, Las Casas, Edward Winslow and John Rolfe, the Declaration of Independence, Frederick Douglass, the SlaveVoyages database; Charles C. Mann, Alfred Crosby, Laurent Dubois, Eric Foner, Ira Berlin, Daniel Richter, Matthew Restall; and the Jamestown excavation report (2013).
src22: Chapter 15, the Mongol Empire (Thai only): the Secret History of the Mongols, al-Juvayni, Rashid al-Din, the Yuan shi, Carpini, William of Rubruck, Marco Polo, Ibn Battuta and Changchun’s disciples; Thomas Allsen, Timothy May, Peter Jackson, Morris Rossabi, David Morgan, Denis Sinor; and the plague DNA study of Spyrou et al. (2022).
src21: Chapter 14, the Islamic world (Thai only): al-Tabari, al-Juvayni, Ibn al-Nadim, Ibn Fadlan, Ibn Sina, the Cairo Geniza (S. D. Goitein), Hugh Kennedy, Dimitri Gutas, Jonathan Bloom, Richard Bulliet, Marshall Hodgson, Carole Hillenbrand, Peter Jackson, and UNESCO files on Samarra, Córdoba and Madinat al-Zahra.
src20: Chapter 13, Suvarnabhumi: the Chinese histories (Liang shu, New Book of Tang, and the quoted reports of Kang Tai), Yijing, and Zhou Daguan’s Customs of Cambodia; Khmer, Mon and Sanskrit inscriptions (as named in the game); the Sukhothai inscriptions; the Dipavamsa and Mahavamsa; the Camadevivamsa and Jinakalamali; UNESCO’s Si Thep nomination (2023); reports of the return of the Golden Boy (2024) and the Phanom Rung lintel (1988); the work of George Cœdès, Michael Vickery, Charles Higham, Dougald O’Reilly, Srisakra Vallibhotama and Phasook Indrawooth; and the excavations at Oc Eo, U Thong, Si Thep and Nakhon Pathom.
src19: Chapter 12, the Ganges: the Pali canon (as named in the game), Jain scriptures, the edicts of Ashoka (E. Hultzsch’s edition), Arrian and Strabo (quoting Megasthenes), the Dipavamsa and Mahavamsa, Richard Gombrich and Heinz Bechert on the Buddha’s dates, A. L. Basham on the Ajivikas, Johannes Bronkhorst (Greater Magadha), Richard Salomon on the Gandharan scrolls (British Library), and the excavations at Sanchi, Bharhut and Piprahwa.
src18: Chapter 11, Rome: Polybius, Cicero, Suetonius, Tacitus, Plutarch, Cassius Dio, the elder and younger Pliny, Pausanias and the Gospels (as named in the game), the Vindolanda tablets, the wall writings of Pompeii, the excavations at Berenike (Sidebotham et al., announced 2023), and the study of Roman concrete (Seymour et al., Science Advances 2023).
src17: Chapter 10, Greece: Herodotus, Thucydides, Plato, Aristotle, Plutarch and Diogenes Laertius (as named in the game), the Copenhagen Polis Centre (inventory of city-states), Josiah Ober and Mogens Hansen (Athenian democracy), Daniel García-Castellanos et al. (the Zanclean flood, Nature 2009), and the Olympias trireme project.
src16: Chapter 09, Olmec: Richard A. Diehl (The Olmecs), Ann Cyphers (San Lorenzo), Ponciano Ortiz and María del Carmen Rodríguez (El Manatí and the Cascajal block, Science 2006), the 2024 rubber-ball study, and the Museum of Anthropology in Xalapa. Ideas about geography, domestic animals and disease draw on many works of environmental history.
src15: Chapter 08, Shang China: David N. Keightley (Sources of Shang History), the oracle-bone collection of the Institute of History and Philology, Academia Sinica, the tomb of Fu Hao (CASS Institute of Archaeology, 1976), the Sanxingdui Museum and the Book of Documents. Legends and stories written by the winners are marked ✦.
src14: Child deaths in pre-modern societies: Volk and Atkinson (2013, Evolution and Human Behavior); Thailand today: UN IGME. Classroom mode: add ?class=1 to the link, or ?room=CODE so the whole class is born as the same person.
src8: Line of travellers: generations assume about 27 years each; distance is measured in straight lines between regions.

shareTpl: I was born a {sp} in {pl} about {y} years ago ({o}), became {ti}, and lived {a} years. On the Earth clock this life lasted {s} seconds · Sapiens in Time
src1: People ever born: Population Reference Bureau (2022) estimates about 117 billion since about 190,000 BCE. After mid-2022 the game adds about 132 million births a year.
src2: Species shares, and when each group lived in each region, are the game’s own estimates drawn from several studies. Several points are still debated.
src3: Death rates follow patterns from studied hunter-gatherer societies, such as Gurven & Kaplan (2007). Life events are a model, not the story of a real person.
src4: Earth clock: Earth’s 4.54 billion years shrunk into one calendar year. One human year is about 0.007 seconds.
src5: Events marked ✦ are legends the game made up, with no evidence behind them. Turn them off with “Realistic only”.
bandMoved: The food ran out. Your band carried you to {r}
